title: Tithonus, consort of Dawn
greek: Τιθωνός (Tithōnos); παρ᾽ ἀγαυοῦ Τιθωνοῖο (par' agauou Tithōnoio)
short: Dawn rises from the bed of Tithonus, the Trojan prince she loved; the line is a formulaic sunrise, used again at the start of Odyssey 5.
body: Tithonus was a Trojan prince whom Eos (Dawn) carried off to be her husband. The Iliad itself only names him: at 20.237 he appears in Aeneas' genealogy as a brother of Priam, son of Laomedon. The famous story attached to him, that Dawn asked Zeus to make him immortal but forgot to ask for eternal youth, so that he shrivelled into endless old age, is first told in the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (218-38), as Leaf notes. Readers who know Tennyson's 'Tithonus' will recognise it. In Homer the couplet is a stock way of opening a new day (the same two lines begin Odyssey 5), but its position here is significant: Book 11 opens the long third day of battle (Books 11-18), the 'great day' on which Zeus' promise to Thetis is fulfilled and Patroclus is drawn toward his death. A mortal lover aging beside an immortal is a quiet emblem of the gulf between gods and men that the whole poem explores.

title: Strife (Eris), sent by Zeus with a 'portent of war'
greek: Ἔρις (Eris); πολέμοιο τέρας (polemoio teras)
short: Zeus sends the goddess Strife to the Greek camp holding a 'portent of war'; her shout makes battle sweeter to the Greeks than going home.
body: Eris, the personified spirit of conflict (sister of Ares at 4.440-3), here acts as Zeus' messenger, a role normally given to Iris. What 'portent of war' (teras) she holds is unknown. Monro lists the guesses: the aegis (once called the portent of Zeus at 5.742), the rainbow (a 'portent of war' at 17.548), lightning (10.5); he finds none of them satisfactory. Leaf too says we cannot tell what Strife holds, though he thinks the aegis the likeliest. Leaf records a curious ancient variant that confuses Eris with Iris, and treats the whole opening (11.1-55) as a late addition, rich in personified battle-spirits. Strife stands on Odysseus' ship, in the centre of the line, so that her shout reaches both flanks, where Aias and Akhilleus have beached their ships; the detail quietly reminds us that Akhilleus is still absent. Lines 13-14 (war became 'sweeter than to return') are borrowed from 2.453-4, where they fit better; ancient editors marked them as suspect, but Leaf thinks they stood here from the first. Strife returns at 11.73, alone among the gods rejoicing in the slaughter.

title: The arming of Agamemnon (an arming type-scene)
greek: ἐδύσετο νώροπα χαλκόν (edyseto nōropa chalkon)
short: Agamemnon's arming follows the fixed Homeric order (greaves, corselet, sword, shield, helmet, spears) and announces his aristeia, his great moment of glory.
body: Homer arms a hero for a major exploit with a recurring 'type-scene' that always runs in the same order: greaves, corselet, sword, shield, helmet, spear(s). The other full examples are Paris (3.330-8), Patroclus (16.131-9) and Akhilleus (19.364-91). The more elaborate the arming, the greater the coming exploit, and Agamemnon's is the most ornate in the poem: a foreign corselet, a shield with Gorgon, Terror and Rout, a three-headed serpent on the baldric. It opens his aristeia (11.91-283), the only stretch of the poem in which the commander-in-chief fights as a great warrior, and it ends abruptly with his wound. Leaf points out that nearly half of lines 1-55 recur elsewhere and that the description is hard to picture as a real object (he calls the author someone describing 'things of which he has no clear conception'); he dates the passage late. For students, the point is structural: Agamemnon's glory is set up only to collapse, and its collapse begins the rout that will bring Patroclus, and then Akhilleus, back into the war.

title: Cinyras (Kinyras), king of Cyprus
greek: Κινύρης (Kinyrēs); ξεινήϊον (xeinēion), guest-gift
short: Agamemnon's corselet was a guest-gift from Cinyras, the legendary priest-king of Cyprus; this is the only mention of the island itself in the Iliad.
body: Cinyras was the great legendary king of Paphos in Cyprus, founder of Aphrodite's cult there and proverbial for wealth (Tyrtaeus couples him with Midas; Pindar, Pythian 2.15, praises him as Apollo's favourite). Leaf explains him as a figure of pre-Greek, Phoenician Cyprus, and notes that his name is usually derived from the Semitic word for lyre (kinnor), an instrument he was said to have invented. The corselet is a xeinēion, a guest-gift, the token of guest-friendship (xenia) that bound aristocrats across distances; Cinyras sends it on hearing the 'great rumour' of the expedition, to win Agamemnon's favour. Later tradition was less flattering: according to Apollodorus (Epitome 3.9) Cinyras promised fifty ships, sent one, and made the rest of clay. Maria Papaioannou argues that the Iliad deliberately suppresses this darker Cypriot story, leaving only a trace in its mention of ships. Leaf notes that, apart from the doubtful case of the name Kypris, this is the only mention of Cyprus in the Iliad, and suggests that the island entered the Greek horizon only after the epic tradition had begun.

title: Cyanus (kyanos), the dark-blue inlay
greek: κύανος (kyanos); μέλανος κυάνοιο (melanos kyanoio)
short: Murray keeps the Greek word: kyanos is a dark-blue material, either lapis lazuli or a blue glass paste imitating it, used in inlaid metalwork.
body: The corselet is inlaid in stripes of kyanos, gold and tin, with three serpents of kyanos rearing toward the neck 'like rainbows'. Leaf, following Lepsius, explains that kyanos covers two things: real lapis lazuli, rare and costly, and an imitation of it in blue glass paste coloured with copper salts, a product for which Cyprus, the copper island, was famous. A frieze of such blue paste was found at Tiryns and matches the 'cornice of kyanos' in Alcinous' palace (Odyssey 7.87). Monro, more cautiously, thought of 'blue steel'. Tin, cheap to us, was rare and precious in early Greece, which is why it keeps company with gold. The same materials decorate the shield of Akhilleus (18.474, 564-5). The epithet 'dark' (melas) reflects the limited Homeric colour vocabulary, which Leaf says hardly distinguishes more than 'red' and 'dark'. Kyanos survives in English 'cyan'.

title: Terror and Rout (Deimos and Phobos) on Agamemnon's shield
greek: Δεῖμός τε Φόβος τε (Deimos te Phobos te); Γοργὼ βλοσυρῶπις (Gorgō blosyrōpis)
short: The Gorgon's face crowns Agamemnon's shield, flanked by the personified powers Terror and Rout; an archaic artist later copied the scene.
body: Deimos (Terror) and Phobos (Rout, panic flight) are the sons and attendants of Ares (cf. 4.440, 13.299, 15.119); the Gorgon's head, which turns beholders to stone, also sits on the aegis (5.741). Placed on a shield, such images are meant to terrify the enemy. Leaf could not reconcile the central boss with the Gorgon and the two figures, and suspected that two descriptions had been combined. He adds a striking piece of evidence for how early Greeks read this very line: Pausanias, describing the carved chest of Cypselus at Olympia (7th-6th century BC), saw Agamemnon fighting Coön over the body of Iphidamas, the episode later in this book, with Phobos on his shield, 'whose head is a lion's', and an inscription calling him 'the Phobos of mortals'. Leaf ranked this among the oldest known illustrations of a literary text. The chest also shows that Phobos was imagined as a monstrous face, much like the Gorgon.

title: Athene and Hera 'thunder' in Agamemnon's honour
greek: ἐπὶ δ᾽ ἐγδούπησαν Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη (epi d' egdoupēsan Athēnaiē te kai Hērē)
short: The two pro-Greek goddesses salute the armed king with a crash of thunder, an unusual act, since thunder is normally Zeus' prerogative.
body: The verb egdoupēsan occurs only here. Leaf observes that it plainly means 'thundered', though elsewhere in Homer thunder belongs to Zeus alone; he also notes that this honour sits awkwardly beside 11.75-8, where all the gods resent Zeus for favouring the Trojans and stay away from the battle. Hera and Athena are the most implacable enemies of Troy (since the Judgement of Paris, alluded to at 24.25-30) and have just been forbidden by Zeus to intervene (Book 8). Their gesture is therefore a short-lived encouragement: within two hundred lines Zeus will send Iris to promise the day to Hector, and Agamemnon will be wounded. The scene also marks the epithet 'king of Mycenae, rich in gold' (polychrysos), a reminder of the wealth that later made Schliemann's Mycenae famous.

title: A rain of bloody dew
greek: ἐέρσας αἵματι μυδαλέας (eersas haimati mydaleas)
short: Zeus sends down dew soaked with blood, a portent of the many deaths to come.
body: The bloody dew is a portent: Zeus, the narrator explains, is about to send 'many a valiant head' to Hades. The only parallel in the Iliad is far more personal: at 16.459-61 Zeus sheds 'bloody raindrops' to honour his own son Sarpedon, whom he cannot save from death at Patroclus' hands. Leaf cross-refers the two passages and remarks that blood-red rain later became a favourite portent in the Roman annals (Livy repeatedly records 'it rained blood'). Such rains have a natural basis, since dust-laden rain can fall red. In Homer, however, the sign is not a warning that men can read and act on: like many Iliadic portents it simply announces, for the audience, what Zeus has already decided. The phrase 'a cry unquenchable' (asbestos boē) a few lines earlier, Leaf notes, departs from the usual picture of the Greeks advancing in silence (3.8, 4.429).

title: Hector like a baneful star (Sirius)
greek: οὔλιος ἀστήρ (oulios astēr)
short: Hector, flashing in and out of the ranks, is compared to a deadly star glimpsed between clouds, almost certainly Sirius, the Dog Star.
body: Oulios ('deadly, baneful') occurs only here in Homer. Leaf identifies the star as Sirius, comparing 22.26-31, where Akhilleus running across the plain shines like the star called 'Orion's Dog', 'brightest, but an evil sign, bringing fever to wretched men'. The simile thus implies both brilliance and danger, appropriate for Hector, who now appears among the front ranks, now among the rear, giving orders. Leaf notes that an ancient variant read 'the morning star' instead, and that some tried to explain oulios as 'hairy', that is, a comet, which he rejects. The pairing is worth noticing: the same star-image marks Hector's rise here and Akhilleus' deadly approach to him in Book 22, a small instance of the poem's long-range design. Hector's armour also 'flashes like the lightning of father Zeus', whose plan now favours him.

title: The reapers simile
greek: οἱ δ᾽ ὥς τ᾽ ἀμητῆρες ἐναντίοι ἀλλήλοισιν (hoi d' hōs t' amētēres enantioi allēloisin)
short: The two armies cut each other down like two bands of reapers working toward each other across a rich man's field.
body: Leaf explains the picture: the reapers start from the two ends of a field and meet in the middle, so that the swathes fall thick on both sides, an image of equal slaughter as the lines close. The 'rich man' (makar, 'blessed') is a landowner with an estate of his own, worked by hired labour; Leaf compares the harvest scene on the king's estate (temenos) on the shield of Akhilleus (18.550-60). The simile belongs to a large Homeric family that sets war against the peaceful work of farming, herding and craft; such similes remind the audience of the world the fighters have left and are destroying. The comparison of killing to harvesting also anticipates the later image of Akhilleus' horses threshing the dead (20.495-503). Immediately after, the fighters 'raged like wolves', and Strife looks on with joy.

anchor: set them free for a ransom
title: Ransom: Akhilleus' earlier mercy to Priam's sons
greek: ἔλυσεν ἀποίνων (elysen apoinōn)
short: Isus and Antiphus had once been captured by Akhilleus and released for ransom; now Agamemnon kills them both without a word.
body: Ransom (apoina) is the regular alternative to killing a captured enemy: the captive is spared and his family pays in bronze, gold and iron. The detail that Akhilleus once seized these two sons of Priam while they herded sheep on Mount Ida and 'set them free for a ransom' (apoinōn is a genitive of price) tells us how Akhilleus fought before the quarrel. He himself recalls it at 21.100-2, speaking to another son of Priam, Lycaon: before Patroclus died, he says, he preferred to spare Trojans and sell them; now none will escape. The contrast is deliberate. In this book it is Agamemnon who is merciless (compare his speech to Menelaus at 6.55-60, urging that no Trojan be spared), while the Akhilleus of the past was the ransoming kind. The final book of the poem turns on ransom, when Akhilleus accepts Priam's gifts for Hector's body.

title: Supplication refused: Peisander and Hippolochus
greek: ζώγρει, Ἀτρέος υἱέ, σὺ δ᾽ ἄξια δέξαι ἄποινα (zōgrei, Atreos huie, sy d' axia dexai apoina)
short: The sons of Antimachus beg for their lives and offer ransom; Agamemnon kills them because their father once urged the murder of Menelaus.
body: Supplication (hiketeia) on the battlefield follows a pattern: the defeated man clasps the victor's knees or, as here from the chariot, begs to be 'taken alive' (zōgrei) and promises ransom. The same line is used by Adrastus at 6.46, whom Menelaus is ready to spare until Agamemnon intervenes. In the Iliad no battlefield suppliant is ever spared. Agamemnon's refusal has a specific motive. Antimachus, bribed with Paris' gold, had opposed returning Helen and had even proposed killing Menelaus and Odysseus when they came to Troy as ambassadors before the war (the embassy is described at 3.205-24). Leaf notes the pointed contrast at 11.137: the young men speak 'gently', but hear an ungentle answer. Agamemnon makes the sons 'pay for the outrage' of their father, then beheads Hippolochus and sends the trunk 'rolling like a round stone' through the crowd. The scene darkens his aristeia: his valour is real, but it is valour without restraint.

anchor: until he come to the well-benched
title: Zeus' message to Hector through Iris
greek: κτείνειν, εἰς ὅ κε νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ἀφίκηται, / δύῃ τ᾽ ἠέλιος (kteinein, eis ho ke nēas eüsselmous aphikētai, dyēi t' ēelios)
short: Zeus tells Hector to hold back until Agamemnon is wounded; then Hector will kill and kill until he reaches the ships at sunset.
body: From the peaks of Ida Zeus sends Iris with a precise timetable. Hector must avoid Agamemnon while he rages; once Agamemnon is wounded and leaves the field, Zeus will give Hector strength 'to slay and slay' until he reaches the ships and the sun sets. This is the working-out of the Plan of Zeus (Dios boulē, 1.5), his promise to Thetis to honour Akhilleus by giving the Trojans victory until the Greeks recognise his worth (1.508-10). Iris repeats the message almost word for word (11.200-9), as Homeric messengers do. The promise defines the shape of the coming books: Hector's advance runs through Books 11-17, and at 17.453-5 Zeus restates it in almost the same words ('until he reaches the well-benched ships and the sun sets'). Hector obeys exactly; when Agamemnon withdraws at 11.280, Hector claims that Zeus has granted him glory (11.288-9).

title: Invocation of the Muses: the turning point
greek: ἔσπετε νῦν μοι, Μοῦσαι Ὀλύμπια δώματ᾽ ἔχουσαι (espete nyn moi, Mousai Olympia dōmat' echousai)
short: A fresh appeal to the Muses marks a moment of special weight: the wounding of Agamemnon, which Leaf calls 'the turning-point of the poem'.
body: The same invocation line opens the Catalogue of Ships (2.484) and recurs at 14.508 and 16.112 (the firing of the ships). Internal invocations mark either a feat of memory (a list of names) or a crucial moment. Leaf comments that this appeal fitly introduces what is really the turning-point of the poem: with the wounding of Agamemnon begins the Greek rout that will move Akhilleus to send Patroclus into battle. Who first faced Agamemnon is a question of fame (kleos) that only the Muses, who are present everywhere and know everything (2.485), can answer reliably. The answer is Iphidamas, a young Thracian-reared son of Antenor, and his story receives the pathos usually given to minor victims: brief biography, marriage, death far from home.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 1: Books I-XII, 2nd ed. (London: Macmillan, 1900), note on 11.218

title: 'A sleep of bronze': death as sleep
greek: κοιμήσατο χάλκεον ὕπνον (koimēsato chalkeon hypnon)
short: Iphidamas 'slept a sleep of bronze': death is a sleep that, unlike ordinary sleep, is hard and unbreakable; Virgil imitates the phrase.
body: Monro calls the phrase an oxymoron: Homeric sleep is normally 'soft', 'sweet' and 'limb-loosening', but this sleep is as hard as metal, the sleep of death. Leaf explains it as though death bound a man with bands he cannot break. Bronze is also the metal of the spear that killed him, so the adjective joins cause and effect. In the Iliad Sleep (Hypnos) and Death (Thanatos) are twin brothers who carry Sarpedon home (16.672, 682). Virgil imitates the line at Aeneid 10.745-6 (ferreus ... somnus, 'an iron sleep'). The following lines add the pathos: Iphidamas is 'unhappy' (oiktros), killed far from his newly-wed wife, 'bearing aid to his townsfolk', without having had any joy of her, though he had paid much for her.

anchor: first he gave an hundred kine
title: Bride-price (hedna): Iphidamas' marriage
greek: ἕδνα (hedna), bride-gifts; κουριδίη ἄλοχος (kouridiē alochos), wedded wife
short: Iphidamas paid a hundred cattle for his bride and promised a thousand sheep and goats; Homeric marriage often involved gifts from the groom to the bride's father.
body: Iphidamas was raised in Thrace by his maternal grandfather Cisseus, who married him to his own daughter, that is, to the boy's aunt, Theano's sister. Leaf comments that this passage 'very clearly shews that marriage was a bargain': the groom pays the father, part at once (a hundred cattle) and part in instalments from the increase of his herds (a thousand head). He sees 'no return' (charis) for what he paid. Homeric marriage customs are not uniform: here and at 22.472 the groom gives hedna, while elsewhere a father may give a daughter 'without bride-price' and even add a dowry, as Agamemnon offers Akhilleus at 9.146-8, and Othryoneus offers military service instead of gifts (13.365-9). Historians still debate how far the poems reflect one real system. The emotional point is clear: a young man who has paid everything for a marriage dies before enjoying it, and the 'twelve beaked ships' he left at Percote will sail home without him.

title: The Eileithyiae: Agamemnon's pain like labour pains
greek: μογοστόκοι Εἰλείθυιαι, Ἥρης θυγατέρες (mogostokoi Eileithuiai, Hērēs thugateres)
short: The pain of Agamemnon's wound is compared to the pangs sent on a woman in labour by the Eileithyiae, Hera's daughters, goddesses of childbirth.
body: The Eileithyiae (one goddess, Eileithyia, in later Greek; plural here and at 19.119) preside over childbirth; Hesiod makes Eileithyia a daughter of Zeus and Hera (Theogony 921-2), and Leaf links her to Hera as goddess of marriage. Their epithet mogostokos ('of hard labour') is of disputed formation, Monro notes. Leaf explains that the pangs are pictured as darts shot into the body, just as grief can be said to 'strike' a man. The simile is remarkable: the commander-in-chief, at the height of his aristeia, is likened to a woman in travail. Some readers find it a deliberate deflation of Agamemnon, who, as Leaf notes, characteristically 'gives way to despondency at the first reverse' (compare 9.27, 14.65-80). Others see simply the poet's search for the most piercing pain known. Either way, the wounded king now leaves the field, and Zeus' timetable for Hector begins.

title: Diomedes' abuse of Paris the archer
greek: τοξότα, λωβητήρ, κέραι ἀγλαέ, παρθενοπῖπα (toxota, lōbētēr, kerai aglae, parthenopipa)
short: Wounded in the foot by Paris' arrow, Diomedes heaps contempt on him: archer, slanderer, proud of his horn (or his curls), girl-ogler.
body: Paris shoots from behind the pillar of Ilus' tomb, the archer's typical safe position, and wounds Diomedes in the foot. Diomedes answers with one of the most compressed insults in Homer. Toxota ('bowman') occurs only here; Leaf notes it is a word of contempt, setting the archer against the man who fights face to face 'in armour'. Lōbētēr means 'slanderer, outrager'. Kerai aglae, 'glorying in your horn', is disputed: most take it as the horn bow, but Aristarchus explained it as a hairstyle wound into a horn-like lock. Monro records both views; Leaf accepts the hairstyle on Helbig's archaeological evidence (hence Murray's 'proud of thy curling locks'). Parthenopipa, 'one who ogles girls', occurs nowhere else in Greek. The insult picks up Hector's earlier abuse of Paris as 'woman-mad' (3.39). Ironically, archers decide much of this book: Paris also wounds Machaon and Eurypylus, and in the end will kill Akhilleus himself (22.359-60).

title: Odysseus' monologue: 'why does my heart debate this?'
greek: ἀλλὰ τίη μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός; (alla tiē moi tauta philos dielexato thymos)
short: Alone and surrounded, Odysseus speaks to his own heart, weighs flight against death, and chooses to stand: the first of the Iliad's great deliberation monologues.
body: Odysseus' speech follows a fixed pattern found in three other moments of crisis: Menelaus over Patroclus' body (17.91-105), Agenor facing Akhilleus (21.553-70) and Hector before his duel (22.99-130). Each speaker addresses his own 'great-hearted spirit' (thymos), sets out the shameful and the dangerous choice, and breaks off with the same line, 'But why does my heart debate these things with me?'. Leaf notes that, apart from 22.385, this line always occurs in speeches introduced by the formula of 11.403. Monro explains the aorist as the tense of impatient questions. Odysseus resolves the dilemma by stating the heroic norm: cowards leave the battle, but the man who would be 'best' must stand firm, whether he is struck or strikes. These scenes are among the clearest windows Homer gives into a character's inner decision, and the comparison between them (Menelaus gives way, while Odysseus, Agenor and Hector stand their ground) is instructive.

title: Denial of burial: the vaunt over Socus
greek: οἰωνοὶ ὠμησταί (oiōnoi ōmēstai), raw-eating birds; κτεριοῦσι (kteriousi), they will give funeral rites
short: Odysseus taunts the dying Socus: his parents will not close his eyes, birds will tear him, whereas Odysseus, if he dies, will be buried by the Greeks.
body: The fear of lying unburied, food for dogs and birds, is announced in the poem's opening lines (1.4-5) and grows into a central theme, culminating in Akhilleus' abuse of Hector's corpse and its ransom in Book 24. Proper burial meant that parents or kin closed the eyes, washed and mourned the body and raised a mound; without it, the dead were thought unable to rest (compare Patroclus' ghost at 23.71-4). Odysseus' vaunt sets the two fates side by side: for Socus, no parents and the beating wings of carrion birds; for himself, the funeral honours (kteriousi) of his comrades. Diomedes has just made a similar boast (11.395: his victim rots with 'more birds than women around him'). Such vaunts are conventional, yet they keep before the audience what is at stake in every death, and they prepare for the moment when this threat is carried out on Hector.

anchor: a leech is of the worth
title: 'A healer is worth many other men'
greek: ἰητρὸς γὰρ ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων (iētros gar anēr pollōn antaxios allōn)
short: When Paris wounds Machaon, the army's surgeon, Idomeneus urges Nestor to rescue him: one doctor is worth many fighting men.
body: 'Leech' is the old English word for physician (iētros). Machaon and his brother Podaleirius, sons of the 'blameless physician' Asclepius, lead a contingent from Thessaly (2.729-33) and serve as the Greek army's doctors. Homeric medicine, as the following lines show, is battlefield surgery: cutting out arrows and spreading soothing drugs (pharmaka). The ancient critics suspected line 515 because it seemed to limit the physician's worth to dressing wounds; Leaf replies that it 'fairly represents the primitive stage of Homeric medicine', and Monro adds that later poets made Machaon the surgeon and Podaleirius the physician. The rescue of Machaon matters for the plot: Akhilleus sees Nestor's chariot carrying him past (11.597-615) and sends Patroclus to ask who is wounded. The healer's wounding thus sets in motion the chain that leads to Patroclus' death.

title: Aias as a lion and as a stubborn ass
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ὄνος παρ᾽ ἄρουραν ἰὼν ἐβιήσατο παῖδας / νωθής (hōs d' hot' onos par' arouran iōn ebiēsato paidas nōthēs)
short: Aias retreats step by step, first like a lion driven from a cattle-fold, then like a lazy donkey that boys cannot beat out of a cornfield.
body: Zeus himself drives Aias back, and Homer gives the retreat two contrasting similes. In the first (548-57), a lion is kept from the fattest cattle by dogs and farmers with spears and torches, and leaves at dawn 'with sullen heart'. In the second (558-62), an ass strays from the road into a field of standing grain; the boys break their cudgels on him but cannot drive him out until he has eaten his fill. Leaf calls it a 'famous simile' and notes that the ass appears nowhere else in Homer, nor even in Hesiod; mules are common. The two images together give both sides of Aias: the noble, unwilling retreat of the lion, and the dogged, almost comic imperviousness of a beast too thick-skinned to hurry. The Trojans' spears stick in his great shield 'longing to glut themselves with flesh', a vivid personification. Aias, the defensive 'wall of the Achaeans', will be the last Greek to hold the ships (15.674-746).

title: Patroclus summoned: 'the beginning of evil'
greek: ἔκμολεν ἶσος Ἄρηϊ, κακοῦ δ᾽ ἄρα οἱ πέλεν ἀρχή (ekmolen isos Arēi, kakou d' ara hoi pelen archē)
short: Patroclus comes out of the hut 'like Ares', and the narrator warns that this was the beginning of his doom; the main plot pivots here.
body: Akhilleus, watching the rout from his ship, calls Patroclus; he comes out 'equal to Ares', and the narrator adds that this moment was 'the beginning of evil' for him. The prolepsis (a look ahead) is rare in so pointed a form; the phrase 'beginning of evil' recalls Paris' ships, 'the beginning of evils' for the Trojans (5.62-3). Leaf records the objections of critics who thought such an allusion to coming events un-Homeric, and judges them not convincing. The comparison to Ares is also ominous: when Patroclus makes his last charge he leaps forward 'like swift Ares' (16.784), and Apollo strikes him down. This is the first time in the poem that we see Patroclus act on his own; Leaf calls him 'the most attractive personality of the Iliad', till now 'but the shadow of Achilles'. From here the errand to Nestor, the meeting with Eurypylus, and Patroclus' plea in Book 16 follow in sequence.

anchor: standing about my knees in prayer
title: 'Now the Achaeans will stand about my knees': the problem of Book 9
greek: νῦν ὀΐω περὶ γούνατ᾽ ἐμὰ στήσεσθαι Ἀχαιοὺς / λισσομένους (nyn oïō peri gounat' ema stēsesthai Achaious lissomenous)
short: Akhilleus expects the Greeks to come begging at his knees, as if the embassy of Book 9 had never happened; scholars have long debated the inconsistency.
body: To clasp someone's knees is the gesture of a suppliant. Akhilleus says that 'now' the Greeks will come to him as suppliants, because need has come upon them that can no longer be borne. Yet in Book 9 Agamemnon's envoys have already come with gifts and pleaded with him. Leaf states bluntly that the words are 'quite inconsistent' with the place of Book 9 in the story, and the analytic critics used the line as evidence that the Embassy was a later insertion. Monro offers a unitarian alternative: Akhilleus may be referring ironically to the Embassy, meaning that the Greeks will come in earnest now, when the Trojans reach the ships. A related puzzle occurs at 16.72-3 and 16.84-6, where Akhilleus speaks as if no gifts had been offered. Students should know both readings: the line either exposes a seam in the poem's composition or shows Akhilleus' wounded pride, which demands a fuller humiliation than Book 9 provided.

title: Hecamede, Nestor's prize of honour
greek: Ἑκαμήδη ἐϋπλόκαμος (Hekamēdē eüplokamos); ἔξελον (exelon), they chose out
short: Hecamede, captured when Akhilleus sacked Tenedos, was chosen out for Nestor by the army as his special prize because he excelled in counsel.
body: Hecamede illustrates how spoils were divided. After a raid, the booty was pooled and distributed, but certain choice items, especially captive women, were 'chosen out' (exelon) for individual leaders as a geras, a prize of honour that expressed public recognition. Hecamede was given to Nestor 'because in counsel he was ever best of all', just as Briseis was the army's gift to Akhilleus (1.162, 1.392) and Chryseis to Agamemnon (1.369). The theft of such a prize is the cause of Akhilleus' wrath. Hecamede, daughter of Arsinous, came from Tenedos, the island off the Trojan coast that Akhilleus sacked in one of his many raids before the poem begins (compare 9.328-9). She reappears only at 14.6, heating bath water for Machaon. Her presence in Nestor's hut, serving a restorative drink, is a domestic counterpart to the slavery of captive women that the poem elsewhere presents as the fate awaiting Troy's wives.

title: Nestor's cup
greek: δέπας περικαλλές (depas perikalles)
short: Nestor's heavy four-handled cup with golden doves, which only he can lift with ease, became a famous object for ancient scholars and modern archaeologists.
body: The cup has four handles, each with two golden doves feeding, and two supports beneath; another man could hardly lift it full, but old Nestor raises it easily, a sign of his surviving strength. Ancient scholars argued about its form at length; Leaf notes that Athenaeus preserves extracts 'of more compass than value'. Schliemann thought he had found it in Shaft Grave IV at Mycenae (16th century BC, now Athens, National Archaeological Museum 412): a gold cup with doves on its handles. Leaf calls that cup the best commentary on the passage, though it has two handles and one dove on each; the identification with Homer's object is now generally rejected. A second 'Nestor's cup', a clay drinking cup from Pithekoussai on Ischia (c. 735-720 BC), bears one of the earliest Greek alphabetic inscriptions, in verse, joking that whoever drinks from it will be seized by desire for Aphrodite. It shows that Nestor's cup was proverbial very early, though scholars debate whether the joke presupposes our Iliad.

title: Pramnian wine and the kykeon (mixed drink)
greek: κυκειῶ (kykeiō, from kykeōn); οἴνῳ Πραμνείῳ (oinōi Pramneiōi)
short: Hecamede mixes a kykeon, a restorative drink of Pramnian wine with grated goat's cheese and barley meal, served with onion and honey.
body: The 'potion' is a kykeōn (from kykaō, 'to stir'), a mixed drink thick enough to be, in Leaf's words, 'a sort of stimulating porridge'. Circe prepares the same mixture, cheese, barley meal and honey in Pramnian wine, for Odysseus' men before adding her drug (Odyssey 10.234-5). A different kykeon, of barley, water and mint, was the ritual drink of Demeter's mysteries (Homeric Hymn to Demeter 208-10). Pramnian wine was a puzzle already in antiquity: Monro notes that the ancient commentators disagreed about its place of origin, and Leaf reports the scholiast's derivation from a mountain in Caria, Galen's description of it as a black, austere wine, and Hehn's guess at a Thracian name, concluding that 'the ancients themselves knew nothing about it'. The scene is one of the poem's rare moments of calm hospitality in the middle of disaster.

title: Nestor's tale of the Pylian-Elean war (a paradigm)
greek: ἀμφὶ βοηλασίῃ (amphi boēlasiēi), over a cattle-raid; ῥύσια (rhysia), reprisals
short: Nestor tells, at great length, how as a youth he led a cattle raid into Elis and won the battle at the Alpheius; the story is meant to shame Akhilleus.
body: This is the longest of Nestor's reminiscences (about ninety lines). Pylos had been crippled when Heracles sacked it and killed eleven of Neleus' twelve sons, leaving only Nestor (11.690-3; compare Apollodorus 2.7.3); the Epeians of Elis exploited its weakness, and Augeias even seized Neleus' prize-winning chariot team. Young Nestor answers with a reprisal raid (rhysia), drives off huge herds, and then wins the pitched battle that follows. Leaf, though he admired the 'lifelike picture of a little border raid', thought it late and 'grotesquely out of place' when Patroclus has just refused to sit down. Modern readers usually see it as a paradigm, a story from the past used to persuade: Nestor fought for his community and shared the spoils fairly, so that no man went 'defrauded of an equal share' (11.705), whereas 'Achilles would alone have profit of his valour' (11.762-3). The pointed contrast with the unfair division that began the quarrel in Book 1 is part of the argument.

title: The Moliones (Actorione), twin sons of Poseidon
greek: Μολίονε (Molione, dual); Ἀκτορίωνε (Aktoriōne)
short: The Moliones, Cteatus and Eurytus, were twin leaders of the Epeians, sons of Actor in name and of Poseidon in fact; Poseidon saves them from Nestor.
body: The twins are named Cteatus and Eurytus, 'sons of Actor', in the Catalogue (2.621), and Nestor recalls at 23.638-42 that they beat him in a chariot race at the funeral games of Amarynceus, one driving, the other using the whip. Monro and Leaf explain the two names: 'Actorione' is a patronymic from their nominal father Actor (brother of Augeias), while 'Molione' probably derives from their mother Molione; their real father is Poseidon, who here wraps them in mist to save them (11.750-2). Leaf adds that they played a great part in the Heracles epics; Pausanias tells how Heracles, unable to defeat them in his war with Augeias, ambushed and killed them at Cleonae (5.2.1). Later poets made them more fantastic still: the lyric poet Ibycus spoke of them born from a silver egg, and other sources describe them as conjoined twins with one body. Homer knows nothing of this.

title: Agamede, who knew all drugs
greek: ξανθὴ Ἀγαμήδη, ἣ τόσα φάρμακα ᾔδη (xanthē Agamēdē, hē tosa pharmaka ēidē)
short: Agamede, Augeias' eldest daughter, 'knew all the drugs the wide earth nourishes'; Leaf saw in her a Homeric counterpart of Medea.
body: Nestor's first victim, Mulius, was married to Agamede, eldest daughter of Augeias, 'who knew all simples that the wide earth nourisheth'. Leaf suggests that she is the Homeric form of Medea, who had not yet been drawn into the Argonaut legend: both are granddaughters of the Sun (Augeias is a son of Helios, as Aeetes, Medea's father, is), and both are famed for skill in drugs; Pindar calls Medea 'the stranger skilled in all drugs' (Pythian 4.233). 'Simples' is Murray's word for medicinal herbs (pharmaka). Drugs in Homer are double-edged, healing or harmful, and are often the knowledge of women from distant or magical places: compare Helen's Egyptian drug at Odyssey 4.219-32 and Circe's in Odyssey 10. The detail fits the medical thread running through this book, from Machaon's wounding to Patroclus' treatment of Eurypylus with a pain-killing root at the end.

title: The fathers' charges: Peleus to Akhilleus, Menoetius to Patroclus
greek: αἰὲν ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων (aien aristeuein kai hypeirochon emmenai allōn); γενεῇ μὲν ὑπέρτερος (geneēi men hyperteros)
short: Peleus told Akhilleus always to be best and pre-eminent; Menoetius told the older Patroclus to advise his nobler friend wisely. Nestor reminds Patroclus of his duty.
body: Nestor recalls the day he and Odysseus came to Phthia to recruit for the war and heard both fathers' farewells. Peleus' charge, 'always to be best and pre-eminent above others', is the same line Glaucus' father gave him (6.208): the competitive heroic ideal in a single verse. Menoetius' charge is different: Akhilleus is higher 'by birth' (as son of a goddess, Leaf explains), but Patroclus is older, and must guide him with counsel. Ancient readers argued over this line; some took 'higher' to mean younger, and Plato's Symposium (180a) insists that Akhilleus was the younger and beardless partner, against Aeschylus' version of their love. Leaf notes that Patroclus' advisory role here is not consistent with Phoenix's claim to be Akhilleus' tutor in Book 9. Nestor's point is persuasive and pointed: 'thus did the old man charge thee, but thou forgettest'. The 'persuasion of a friend' is the lever by which the plot now moves.

title: Nestor's plan: Patroclus in Akhilleus' armour
greek: καί τοι τὰ ἃ τεύχεα δότω (kai toi ta ha teuchea dotō); φάος Δαναοῖσι (phaos Danaoisi), a light to the Danaans
short: Nestor proposes that, if Akhilleus will not fight, he lend Patroclus his armour, so that the Trojans mistake him for Akhilleus and the Greeks win a respite.
body: This proposal sets the tragic plot of Books 16-22 in motion. Patroclus will repeat it to Akhilleus almost word for word (16.36-45), and Akhilleus will accept it. Nestor hopes Patroclus may be 'a light (phaos) of deliverance' to the Greeks, a common Homeric metaphor for rescue. The plan works too well: the disguise frightens the Trojans, but Patroclus goes beyond Akhilleus' limits, is killed by Apollo, Euphorbus and Hector, and Hector strips the armour and wears it (17.125, 17.192-7). Akhilleus must then receive new arms from Hephaestus (Book 18), and he kills Hector in his own former armour. Leaf notes that Aristarchus doubted the final lines here as more at home in Book 16. Nestor also offers Akhilleus an escape: if he is avoiding 'some oracle' revealed by his mother, let him at least send Patroclus. The audience knows the prophecy (9.410-16): a short life with glory, or a long one without.

anchor: the most righteous of the Centaurs
title: Cheiron, the most just of the Centaurs
greek: Χείρων, δικαιότατος Κενταύρων (Cheirōn, dikaiotatos Kentaurōn)
short: Patroclus learned healing from Akhilleus, who learned it from Cheiron, the wise Centaur who also taught Asclepius.
body: The Centaurs, half-man and half-horse, are usually savage: in the Iliad they are the wild 'beast-men' of the mountains whom the Lapiths destroyed (1.262-8). Cheiron is the exception. Leaf glosses dikaiotatos as 'the most civilized', the one most at home with dikē, traditional order. He taught medicine to Asclepius (4.219) and gave Peleus the ash spear that only Akhilleus can wield (16.143-4). Monro calls this line 'doubtless the source' of the later stories of Akhilleus' education by Cheiron, which Pindar tells at length (Nemean 3.43-58). The scholia already noticed that it sits uneasily with Phoenix's claim in Book 9 to have raised Akhilleus. The chain of teaching (Cheiron to Akhilleus to Patroclus) gives Patroclus a healer's skill, which he now uses on Eurypylus, cutting out the arrow and applying a bitter, pain-killing root. His compassion, delaying his errand for a wounded comrade, defines his character before his great day in Book 16.
